rationale: The title and abstract describe a non-empirical commentary/overview advocating a One Health and Environmental Health approach (spanning WASH practices, pharmaceutical/solid waste disposal, and food hygiene) to prevent antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in LMICs. It reports no empirical data, study design, or systematic review (E05), measures no household/community water or sanitation service access outcome, and only mentions 'enforcement of legislation' in passing as a general practitioner role in AMR control rather than analysing a legal or administrative mechanism governing water or sanitation service access.
plain_vs_narrow_note: Excluded under both narrow and plain Criterion 2 readings: this is a non-empirical conceptual commentary/perspective on the role of Environmental Health (WASH, solid waste, and food safety) in preventing antimicrobial resistance, with no empirical study or systematic synthesis and no examination of mechanisms governing household/community water or sanitation service access.

evidence_quotes.quote: The role of Environmental Health in preventing antimicrobial resistance in low- and middle-income countries

Environmental Health, specifically water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH), waste management, and food hygiene and safety, are key components of One Health needed to prevent the spread of antimicrobial-resistant microorganisms particularly in LMICs

Working with other professionals in One Health, Environmental Health Practitioners have a key role in reducing the spread of AMR including health education and promotion, surveillance, enforcement of legislation, and research.
